findings.text: Within a few sentences a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. The page does this part well.
findings.source: Opening paragraph (class "lede"): "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: Athena's main promise is a commit you can trace to its models, cost and verdict. The one place that would show this is the second section on the page, and it shows an error. A newcomer meets a broken-looking section early and never sees an example of what Athena produces.
findings.source: Heading "Check it on a real job": "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: This is Athena's home page, but almost all of it is about firstmate, a different project. "Start here" teaches firstmate, not Athena. A newcomer has to work out from the third lede paragraph that the page is a demo study rather than Athena's documentation.
findings.source: Page title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and heading "Start here": "The three parts below say what firstmate is..."

findings.text: This link speaks to a newcomer as "your decision" but is meant for the project owner. It is confusing to see it near the top for someone visiting for the first time.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Even the default core track uses exit codes, lock contention and pending-close records. A newcomer gets little from this detail unless they already care how firstmate works inside.
findings.source: Heading "When things go wrong, and what is not limited": "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: the prerequisites, clone, setup and a first command, with a note on which repository it acts on. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Heading "Next steps": "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\"... press Enter to run it on that repository."

findings.text: The page says two different models are used and that each step has a cost. It never says which accounts or API keys are needed, or roughly what a run costs. A newcomer cannot judge what it takes to try Athena before installing.
findings.source: Heading "Next steps" prerequisites: "Claude Code, or npm to install it." vs lede: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: Each statement links through a claim id to the exact lines in firstmate's files. This is a convincing, checkable demonstration of the "traceable" idea, for a reader who follows a link.
findings.source: Lede: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it" and heading "Claims and sources"
